title: Actus reus and omissions
rule: Actus reus is the external element of an offence: conduct, prohibited result or circumstances. Usually there is no liability for failing to act unless a legal duty exists, for example a duty from statute, contract, relationship, voluntary assumption of care, or creation of danger.
cases: R v Miller — creating a dangerous situation may give rise to a duty to act; R v Stone and Dobinson — assuming care can establish a duty; R v Pittwood — contractual duty.
example: A person accidentally starts a small fire, notices it, then leaves. Explain why the omission after noticing the danger matters.

title: Causation
rule: For result crimes the prosecution proves factual causation (but for the defendant’s conduct would the result have occurred?) and legal causation (a significant operating cause). An independent intervening act may break the chain.
cases: R v White — but-for test; R v Smith — operating and substantial cause; R v Cheshire — medical treatment rarely breaks chain; R v Blaue — take victim as found.
example: A victim refuses medical treatment after an injury. Consider the thin-skull rule and whether causation remains.

title: Mens rea: intention and recklessness
rule: Direct intention means a result is the defendant’s aim. Oblique intention may be found when death or serious injury is a virtual certainty and the defendant appreciates that fact; the jury is entitled, not required, to infer intention. Subjective recklessness requires awareness of a risk and unreasonable taking of it.
cases: R v Woollin — virtual certainty; R v Cunningham — subjective recklessness; R v G and another — awareness of risk.
example: A person knows a harmful result is virtually certain but says it was not their purpose. Explain oblique intention.
pitfall: Do not simply name a case: explain its principle and connect it to the facts.

title: Negligence, transferred malice and coincidence
rule: Negligence assesses departure from required care. Transferred malice may transfer intent between victims of the same type of offence. Actus reus and mens rea must coincide, although a continuing act or series of acts can satisfy the rule.
cases: R v Latimer — transferred malice; R v Pembliton — limits; Fagan v MPC — continuing act; Thabo Meli v R — single transaction.
example: A driver accidentally drives onto an officer’s foot and then deliberately refuses to move. Apply the continuing-act principle.

title: Strict liability and criminal law theory
rule: Some offences dispense with proof of mens rea for at least one element. Courts generally presume mens rea unless legislation clearly displaces it. Evaluate public protection, efficiency, fairness and fault. Criminalisation should consider harm, autonomy, fair labelling and certainty.
cases: Sweet v Parsley — presumption of mens rea; Gammon (Hong Kong) Ltd v AG — guidance on strict liability.

title: Murder
rule: Murder is the unlawful killing of a human being under the King’s peace with intention to kill or cause grievous bodily harm. Prove actus reus, causation and mens rea. Intention to cause serious harm is sufficient, even if death was not intended.
cases: R v Vickers — intent to cause GBH sufficient; R v Woollin — oblique intention; R v Malcherek and Steel — life support and causation.
example: A defendant intends to cause serious injury and the victim dies. Explain why an intention to kill is not essential.

title: Loss of control
rule: A partial defence reducing murder to voluntary manslaughter. There must be loss of self-control, a qualifying trigger (fear of serious violence or things said/done of exceptionally grave character causing justifiable sense of being seriously wronged), and a person of the same age and sex with normal tolerance and self-restraint might have reacted similarly. Revenge excludes the defence. Loss need not be sudden.
cases: R v Clinton — sexual infidelity may be contextual evidence; R v Dawes — limitations; R v Jewell — loss of control.
example: An accused acts after prolonged provocation. Examine qualifying triggers, revenge and objective test.

title: Assault and battery
